## Introduction

In this week’s task, we will examine and compare four kinds of estimates for the number of copies of a cell.

We will try to highlight the pros and cons of each method and also check their influence on different areas of the chromosome, considering the logic of the GC effect.

## Setup - Preliminary part

To make the process easier, we added 0 values to each file to represent 0 reads in a cell or 0 GC count in every cell. This is only for the purpose of ensuring equal cell size along the entire 250M length of the chromosome.

We will eventually clean the data and remove outliers so that the illogical parts (0 GC count in every cell) will not matter.

As requested, we created 100k cells for the cancer sample and healthy sample, each cell containing 2.5k bases, and did the same for the GC content.

```{r}
# Pad each dataset with zeros to reach 2.5 million elements
desired_length <- 2500000

# Function to pad a vector with zeros
pad_with_zeros <- function(data, desired_length) {
  current_length <- length(data)
  if (current_length < desired_length) {
    data <- c(data, rep(0, desired_length - current_length))
  }
  return(data)
}

# Apply padding to each dataset
GC_100 <- pad_with_zeros(GC_100, desired_length)
reads_100_A1 <- pad_with_zeros(reads_100_A1, desired_length)
reads_100_B1 <- pad_with_zeros(reads_100_B1, desired_length)

# Function to sum every 'n' elements into a new vector
sum_every_n <- function(data, n) {
  new_length <- length(data) %/% n
  new_data <- numeric(new_length)
  for (i in 1:new_length) {
    start_idx <- (i - 1) * n + 1
    end_idx <- i * n
    new_data[i] <- sum(data[start_idx:end_idx])
  }
  return(new_data)
}

# Sum every 25 elements for each dataset
new_GC_100 <- (sum_every_n(GC_100, 25))/25
new_reads_100_A1 <- sum_every_n(reads_100_A1, 25)
new_reads_100_B1 <- sum_every_n(reads_100_B1, 25)
```

## Part A - Comparing Estimation Methods

Before we begin with our methods, we need to create the partition of the data that separates the 25M - 30M region in terms of cells and the 75M - 80M region in terms of cells.

We calculated and found:

25M - 30M location on the chromosome -\> 10K - 12K cells

75M - 80M location on the chromosome -\> 30K - 32K cells

```{r}
# Create the 25M - 30M location dataset
loc_GC_100_A <- new_GC_100[10000:11999]
loc_reads_A1_A <- new_reads_100_A1[10000:11999]
loc_reads_B1_A <- new_reads_100_B1[10000:11999]

loc_25m_30m <- data.frame(
  GC_Content = loc_GC_100_A,
  Reads_A1 = loc_reads_A1_A,
  Reads_B1 = loc_reads_B1_A
)

# Create the 75M - 80M location dataset
loc_GC_100_B <- new_GC_100[30000:31999]
loc_reads_A1_B <- new_reads_100_A1[30000:31999]
loc_reads_B1_B <- new_reads_100_B1[30000:31999]

loc_75m_80m <- data.frame(
  GC_Content = loc_GC_100_B,
  Reads_A1 = loc_reads_A1_B,
  Reads_B1 = loc_reads_B1_B
)
```

### Question 1 - Just Median Correction :

Our first method is a simple median correction with no GC correction whatsoever.

We created histograms for both location regions and for both sample estimators in each group (cancer and healthy).

```{r}
# Just med correction to 25m - 30m health
loc_25m_30m$med_cor_health <- loc_25m_30m$Reads_B1 / median(loc_25m_30m$Reads_B1)

# Just med correction to 25m - 30m cancer
loc_25m_30m$med_cor_cancer <- loc_25m_30m$Reads_A1 / median(loc_25m_30m$Reads_A1)

# Set up the plotting area for a 1x2 grid
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Plot histograms 
hist(loc_25m_30m$med_cor_health, breaks = 15, main = "", xlab = "Estimate", col = "steelblue")
title(main = "Health", line = 0.5, cex.main = 1.5)

hist(loc_25m_30m$med_cor_cancer, breaks = 15, main = "", xlab = "Estimate", col = "coral")
title(main = "Cancer", line = 0.5, cex.main = 1.5)

# Add a headline 
mtext("Median Correction Only: 25M - 30M", outer = TRUE, cex = 1.2, line = -1)
```

```{r}
# Just med correction to 75m - 80m health
loc_75m_80m$med_cor_health <- loc_75m_80m$Reads_B1 / median(loc_75m_80m$Reads_B1)

# Just med correction to 75m - 80m cancer
loc_75m_80m$med_cor_cancer <- loc_75m_80m$Reads_A1 / median(loc_75m_80m$Reads_A1)

# Set up the plotting area for a 1x2 grid
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Plot histograms 
hist(loc_75m_80m$med_cor_health, breaks = 15, main = "", xlab = "Estimate", col = "steelblue")
title(main = "Health", line = 0.5, cex.main = 1.5)

hist(loc_75m_80m$med_cor_cancer, breaks = 15, main = "", xlab = "Estimate", col = "coral")
title(main = "Cancer", line = 0.5, cex.main = 1.5)

# Add headline 
mtext("Median Correction Only: 75M - 80M", outer = TRUE, cex = 1.2, line = -1)
```

Here, we added a location comparison plot that will serve as a benchmark for the effect of GC in different locations:

```{r}
# Prepare the data for plotting
loc_25m_30m$Index <- 1:nrow(loc_25m_30m)
loc_75m_80m$Index <- (nrow(loc_25m_30m) + 1):(nrow(loc_25m_30m) + nrow(loc_75m_80m))

# Adjust the margins 
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

# Plot health 
plot(loc_25m_30m$Index, loc_25m_30m$med_cor_health, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 4000), cex = 0.2)
points(loc_75m_80m$Index, loc_75m_80m$med_cor_health, pch = 16, col = "black", cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(500, 2.9, "Health", pos = 4, cex = 1.2, col = "steelblue")  

# Plot cancer 
plot(loc_25m_30m$Index, loc_25m_30m$med_cor_cancer, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 4000), cex = 0.2)
points(loc_75m_80m$Index, loc_75m_80m$med_cor_cancer, pch = 16, col = "black", cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(500, 2.9, "Cancer", pos = 4, cex = 1.2, col = "coral")  
```

**Results Explanations:**

For our first method, we obtained pretty similar plots in terms of location when comparing cancer to healthy samples. However, when we compare the same sample across different locations (the location plot), we can see that the trends are not the same.

### Question 2 - One sample:

Now, we make the preparations for the one-sample estimator.

We want to apply the GC effect to each sample separately (this is why it is called “one sample”).

Of course, we will also check how the location is affected by it because, as we already know, the GC content is not the same across the entire chromosome.

```{r}
# Fit the regression model 25m -30M health 
f_25m_30m_health <- lm(Reads_B1 ~ bs(GC_Content, degree = 3), data = loc_25m_30m)

loc_25m_30m$predicted_values_health <- predict(f_25m_30m_health)

# Fit the regression model 25m -30M cancer 
f_25m_30m_cancer <- lm(Reads_A1 ~ bs(GC_Content, degree = 3), data = loc_25m_30m)

loc_25m_30m$predicted_values_can <- predict(f_25m_30m_cancer)

# Fit the regression model 75m -80M health 
f_75m_80m_health <- lm(Reads_B1 ~ bs(GC_Content, degree = 3), data = loc_75m_80m)

loc_75m_80m$predicted_values_health <- predict(f_75m_80m_health)

# Fit the regression model 75m -80M cancer 
f_75m_80m_cancer <- lm(Reads_A1 ~ bs(GC_Content, degree = 3), data = loc_75m_80m)

loc_75m_80m$predicted_values_can <- predict(f_75m_80m_cancer)

# One sample GC corrcet 
one_sample_correct = function(samp, preds, eps) {
  one_correct = (samp+eps)/(preds+eps)
  adj_med = 1/median(one_correct)
  return(adj_med * one_correct)
}

eps = 1

# The 25m -30m case
corrected_health_25m_30m = one_sample_correct (loc_25m_30m$Reads_B1,loc_25m_30m$predicted_values_health,eps)

uncorrected_health_25m_30m = one_sample_correct(loc_25m_30m$Reads_B1,rep(1,length(loc_25m_30m$Reads_B1)),eps)

corrected_cancer_25m_30m = one_sample_correct (loc_25m_30m$Reads_A1,loc_25m_30m$predicted_values_can,eps)

uncorrected_cancer_25m_30m = one_sample_correct(loc_25m_30m$Reads_A1,rep(1,length(loc_25m_30m$Reads_A1)),eps)

# The 75m -80m case
corrected_health_75m_80m = one_sample_correct (loc_75m_80m$Reads_B1,loc_75m_80m$predicted_values_health,eps)

uncorrected_health_75m_80m = one_sample_correct(loc_75m_80m$Reads_B1,rep(1,length(loc_75m_80m$Reads_B1)),eps)

corrected_cancer_75m_80m = one_sample_correct (loc_75m_80m$Reads_A1,loc_75m_80m$predicted_values_can,eps)

uncorrected_cancer_75m_80m = one_sample_correct(loc_75m_80m$Reads_A1,rep(1,length(loc_75m_80m$Reads_A1)),eps)
```

Here, we create the plot by location in the same way we did earlier.

We will have one plot of corrected vs. uncorrected for the cancer sample and one for the healthy sample.

```{r}
# Adjust the margins 
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))

# Plot corrected data
plot(loc_25m_30m$Index, corrected_cancer_25m_30m, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 4000), cex = 0.2)
points(loc_75m_80m$Index, corrected_cancer_75m_80m, pch = 16, col = "black", cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(500, 2.9, "Corrected - cancer", pos = 4, cex = 1.2, col = "black")

# Plot uncorrected data
plot(loc_25m_30m$Index, uncorrected_cancer_25m_30m, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 4000), cex = 0.2)
points(loc_75m_80m$Index, uncorrected_cancer_75m_80m, pch = 16, col = "black", cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(500, 2.9, "Uncorrected - cancer", pos = 4, cex = 1.2, col = "black")
```

```{r}
# Adjust the margins 
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))

# Plot corrected data
plot(loc_25m_30m$Index, corrected_health_25m_30m, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 4000), cex = 0.2)
points(loc_75m_80m$Index, corrected_health_75m_80m, pch = 16, col = "black", cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(500, 2.9, "Corrected - health", pos = 4, cex = 1.2, col = "black")

# Plot uncorrected data
plot(loc_25m_30m$Index, uncorrected_health_25m_30m, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", ylab = "", xlim = c(0, 4000), cex = 0.2)
points(loc_75m_80m$Index, uncorrected_health_75m_80m, pch = 16, col = "black", cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(500, 2.9, "Uncorrected - health", pos = 4, cex = 1.2, col = "black")
```

**Results Explanations:**

It looks like the main point we are trying to show is evident: when we apply the one-sample correction, the problematic areas in terms of the number of copy estimators (like the 26.8M area) are much more obvious in the plot.

**Note:** In class, we were able to show it even more clearly, probably due to some mistake in our code or more accurate filtering of outliers performed in class.

### Question 3 - Two sample, No GC:

```{r}
# Two sample correction function
two_sample_correct_e = function(tumor, normal,eps = 1) {
  two_correct = (tumor+eps)/(normal+eps)
  two_correct_aft_med = two_correct/median(two_correct,na.rm=TRUE)
  return(two_correct_aft_med)
}

# Two sample, No GC: 25M - 30M
two_samp_No_GC_25m_30m <- two_sample_correct_e(uncorrected_cancer_25m_30m,uncorrected_health_25m_30m) 

# Two sample, No GC: 75M - 80M
two_samp_No_GC_75m_80m <- two_sample_correct_e(uncorrected_cancer_75m_80m,uncorrected_health_75m_80m) 
```

```{r}
# Combine the data for plotting
combined_data <- data.frame(
  Index = c(loc_25m_30m$Index, loc_75m_80m$Index),
  TwoSampleNoGC = c(two_samp_No_GC_25m_30m, two_samp_No_GC_75m_80m),
  Location = rep(c("25M-30M", "75M-80M"), c(length(two_samp_No_GC_25m_30m), length(two_samp_No_GC_75m_80m)))
)

# Set up the plotting area 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))

# Plot two sample, No GC 
plot(combined_data$Index, combined_data$TwoSampleNoGC, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", xlim = c(0, max(combined_data$Index)), cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(max(combined_data$Index) / 4, 2.8, "Two Sample - No GC", pos = 3, cex = 1, col = "black")
```

### Question 4 - Two sample, With GC:

```{r}
# Two sample, With GC: 25M - 30M
two_samp_with_GC_25m_30m <- two_sample_correct_e(corrected_cancer_25m_30m,corrected_health_25m_30m)

# Two sample, With GC: 75M - 80M
two_samp_with_GC_75m_80m <- two_sample_correct_e(corrected_cancer_75m_80m,corrected_health_75m_80m)
```

```{r}
# Combine the data for plotting
combined_data_with_gc <- data.frame(
  Index = c(loc_25m_30m$Index, loc_75m_80m$Index),
  TwoSampleWithGC = c(two_samp_with_GC_25m_30m, two_samp_with_GC_75m_80m),
  Location = rep(c("25M-30M", "75M-80M"), c(length(two_samp_with_GC_25m_30m), length(two_samp_with_GC_75m_80m)))
)

# Set up the plotting area 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))

# Plot two sample, With GC 
plot(combined_data_with_gc$Index, combined_data_with_gc$TwoSampleWithGC, ylim = c(0, 3), pch = 16, col = "black",
     xlab = "Index", xlim = c(0, max(combined_data_with_gc$Index)), cex = 0.2)
abline(h = 1, col = "blue", lty = 1)
abline(v = nrow(loc_25m_30m), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(max(combined_data_with_gc$Index) / 4, 2.8, "Two Sample - With GC", pos = 3, cex = 1, col = "black")
```

**Results Explanations:**

When we look at the results of the “Two sample” methods, we find that some areas we might have thought were problematic (like the 26.8M area) are “canceled out” by the estimation noise combined from both samples, which might disqualify it as a problematic area in terms of the number of copies.

On the other hand, we revealed that the 28.75M area, even with the GC effect taken into consideration, is lower than the expected value of one copy, which might indicate a true copy number problem in this area of the chromosome.

## Part B - Quantitative measure <span class="math inline">\\MAD\\</span>

As a quantitative measure, we chose the <span class="math inline">\\MAD\\</span> - mean absolute deviation.

What it does is take the “a” estimates we got, subtract 1 from each, and then take the absolute value (because we don’t care in which direction it deviates from 1 right now, just that it is far from 1).

We did this only for the Two sample methods: with and without GC correction.

```{r}
# Function to calculate MAD for each cell
calculate_mad_per_cell <- function(observed, expected) {
  mad_per_cell <- abs(observed - expected)
  return(mad_per_cell)
}

# Expected value
expected_value <- 1

# Calculate MAD per cell for two sample methods
mad_two_sample_no_gc_25m_30m <- calculate_mad_per_cell(two_samp_No_GC_25m_30m, expected_value)
mad_two_sample_no_gc_75m_80m <- calculate_mad_per_cell(two_samp_No_GC_75m_80m, expected_value)
mad_two_sample_with_gc_25m_30m <- calculate_mad_per_cell(two_samp_with_GC_25m_30m, expected_value)
mad_two_sample_with_gc_75m_80m <- calculate_mad_per_cell(two_samp_with_GC_75m_80m, expected_value)

# Combine MAD values with their indexes
mad_two_sample_no_gc_25m_30m_df <- data.frame(Index = loc_25m_30m$Index, MAD = mad_two_sample_no_gc_25m_30m)
mad_two_sample_no_gc_75m_80m_df <- data.frame(Index = loc_75m_80m$Index, MAD = mad_two_sample_no_gc_75m_80m)
mad_two_sample_with_gc_25m_30m_df <- data.frame(Index = loc_25m_30m$Index, MAD = mad_two_sample_with_gc_25m_30m)
mad_two_sample_with_gc_75m_80m_df <- data.frame(Index = loc_75m_80m$Index, MAD = mad_two_sample_with_gc_75m_80m)

# Function to get top 10 MAD values
get_top_10 <- function(df) {
  df[order(df$MAD, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10], ]
}

# Print top 10 MAD values for each method
print("Top 10 MAD values for Two Sample No GC 25M-30M:")
```

**Results Explanations:**

The <span class="math inline">\\MAD\\</span> confirmed a bit of what we thought.

When we look at the “Top 10 MAD values for Two Sample No GC 25M-30M,” we can see that the 26.8M area is the main concern.

However, when we compare it to the “Top 10 MAD values for Two Sample With GC 25M-30M”, we find, as before, that the 28.75M area is probably the area we want to keep an eye on.

**Note:** The indexes in the lists above are not the locations on the chromosome itself. We need to keep in mind the adjustment to the right location whenever reading them.

## Part C - Pros & Cons

- Correcting a single sample for GC content helps fix distortions in read counts caused by varying GC content in the DNA.It’s also pretty easy and straightforward since it involves just one sample.However,it only corrects biases in that one sample, and only depends on it, which might not reflect broader trends.

- Comparing two samples without GC correction highlights differences in copy number variations, canceling out some systematic biases,mostly useful for comparing conditions like cancer vs. healthy.However, GC bias remains unaddressed, potentially affecting the results.

- Correcting two samples for GC content before comparing them handles well with both within-sample and between-sample biases, making it great for comparing cancer vs. healthy. However, it’s more complex and time-consuming, requiring extra computational resources.

- When we want to take a look on application to other chromosomal areas,and if our analysis is correct, we believe that the two-sample method revealed the 28.75M area, which we probably would not have found without it. The problem with these methods is that we are not sure if the elimination of the 26.8M area as a problematic area, which we identified in the first method, is a correct elimination.

## Short summary

This week’s lab really emphasizes the importance of choosing the estimation model that we believe is most relevant to our case.

For example, in the 28.75M area, we can’t say for sure that it’s an area with a shortage of helices if we are not completely sure of our process, our assumptions, and our estimation model.
